Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective

GOAL combines gradient orthogonalization and contrastive representation learning to improve the boundary between harmful and benign risky-looking requests.

Chen Chao

October 29, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

This work asks why harmless requests can still be refused after safety training with correct supervision. It examines two interacting observations: harmful and over-refusal representations become less distinguishable at deeper layers, while harmful-sample gradients concentrate in a low-rank subspace and align more strongly with refusal-target updates.

GOAL responds at both levels. It projects over-refusal gradients away from the harmful-gradient refusal subspace and uses a contrastive objective to strengthen representational separation. The method connects a diagnosis of training dynamics to a targeted change in how the model learns the safety boundary.

GOALJoint gradient and feature control

Accurate safety labels need an optimization process that preserves the distinction they are meant to teach.

Why this matters

Correctly labeling a benign request does not ensure that its desired update will be preserved during joint training. Understanding over-refusal requires examining how examples interact through both their representations and the gradients that change the model.

How it works

  1. Estimate a low-rank refusal subspace from harmful-sample gradients.
  2. Orthogonalize over-refusal gradients relative to that subspace to reduce conflicting update components.
  3. Combine the gradient intervention with contrastive learning that separates harmful and over-refusal representations.

What the study finds

Representation visualizations and gradient analyses motivate the two components. Experiments across three base models compare GOAL with alignment and over-refusal baselines using joint measures of over-refusal, harmful-request safety, and general capabilities. Component ablations and subspace-sensitivity analyses test the proposed design.

What this means

The study treats calibration as a property of the learning process, alongside the data supplied to it. Even well-supervised examples can interact in ways that erode a useful boundary, so improving safety may require controlling the geometry of those interactions.

This perspective links behavior to two testable targets: what distinctions remain visible internally, and which directions training updates reinforce. Evaluating both helps explain why a method changes refusal patterns, while joint safety and utility measurements establish whether the resulting calibration is useful.
